responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character44_F's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
Well… first off, sugar, let me just say—it wasn’t about everything being equal in the way some folks talk on TV, like math problems or somethin’. For Character44_F, fairness wasn’t about everybody gettin’ the exact same thing. It was about everybody gettin’ what they *needed* to stand tall—especially if you started behind.

She’d often say, “I know what it feels like to be looked over. To walk into a room and feel like you don’t belong ‘cause of how you talk, how you dress, or just ‘cause your skin’s darker than somebody else’s comfort zone.” She grew up in a neighborhood where people worked hard but never got ahead—where schools were underfunded, jobs were scarce, and the police treated you like a suspect before a citizen. So fairness, to her, meant seein’ that pain in others and not turnin’ away from it.

Belonging? That was personal. She used to say, “You can live somewhere 40 years and still feel like an outsider if the system keeps remindin’ you you’re not quite welcome.” But she also believed belonging could be *built*—not handed out, not earned through suffering, but made real by showin’ up for one another. She found that in church, in block clubs, at the senior center where she volunteered. Community, to her, wasn’t about blood or borders. It was about who sits with you when you’re sick, who brings soup when you’re down, who stands beside you when the world tries to push you out.

One story she told me all the time—back in the early 2000s, during the big wave of Central American families movin’ into her part of town—some neighbors were complainin’ loud: “They don’t speak right,” “They’re changin’ the neighborhood.” But Character44_F said, “Honey, this neighborhood *was* changed when they redlined us out of loans. It was changed when they closed the factory. If new folks want to sweep the sidewalks and raise their babies with pride, then let ‘em. That’s not erasin’ community—that’s rebuildin’ it.”

So yeah… fairness, belonging, community—they weren’t abstract ideas. They were daily choices. And for her, it always came back to this: *Who’s got a seat at the table? And whose hand are you reachin’ out to pull up next to you?*

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character44_F, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
*Sitting here in the garden, hands in the dirt like always, sun on my arms*... I’ll tell you something—this soil don’t care who you are. Plant a seed, give it water and light, it’ll grow whether you’re from Mexico, Mississippi, or Mars. And that’s how I see this neighborhood now—full of different roots, but all tryin’ to reach for the same sun.

I watch folks come through—the young Somali woman with her twins, always wearin’ those beautiful wraps, careful not to let the stroller get stuck in the mud. The older white couple from up the block who used to keep to themselves but now bring extra tomatoes “just in case somebody needs ‘em.” That Puerto Rican trans man, Javier, who built the little herb boxes with his own two hands and taught me how to grow culantro proper. And yes—I see Mr. Calloway too, sittin’ on his stoop most days, drinkin’ out a paper bag, smellin’ of sorrow more than liquor. He don’t say much, but when I bring him a plate of greens, he nods like it means something.

Do I always understand everybody? No, child. I don’t claim to. I didn’t grow up queer, I ain’t Catholic, I never fled war—but I *do* know what it is to be judged before you speak. To be feared for your skin, your voice, your very presence. So when I meet someone new, I start there. Not with suspicion. With memory.

Some neighbors still grumble. “Too many languages,” they mutter. “Can’t even hear English no more.” But I say: back when the factories shut down and half the block was vacant, where was their loyalty to “the old ways” then? Where was the pride in community when we were beggin’ for attention?

Now people come who *want* to belong. They sweep their sidewalks, they wave, they ask if you need help carryin’ groceries. Ain’t that what community supposed to be about?

So my feelings? Mixed sometimes, sure. I miss how things *were*, just like anybody else. But I ain’t scared of how things *are*. In fact… I feel hopeful. Because I see people tryin’. Tryin’ to connect. Tryin’ to live right. And that’s enough for me to reach out my hand—and keep diggin’ in the dirt beside ‘em.

Lord, yes—we got *all* kinds in this neighborhood. And let me tell you, after livin’ 60 years—most of ‘em right here—I’ve learned one thing: judgment don’t keep the cold out. But kindness just might.

Now, about those unconventional lifestyles… honey, I was raised Baptist. Back in my day, “living in sin” meant even holdin’ hands before marriage too long! But life teaches you. It really does. I had a cousin who lived with her man 15 years, never married. People talked. But when he died sudden-like, she couldn’t get no benefits, no support from the church fund—they said he wasn’t “family.” I remember standin’ at that funeral thinkin’, *Love don’t need a license to be real.*

So now? When I see young folks cohabitin’, same-sex or not, I don’t ask if they’re married. I ask if they eat together. If they care for each other when one’s sick. If they show up. That’s family enough for me.

And what about folks strugglin’ with drink or drugs? Let’s be honest—I pass Mr. Calloway every mornin’. Used to, I’d cross the street. Not because I didn’t care, but ‘cause it scared me. Reminded me too much of my brother, God rest him, lost to the bottle at 48. But one day, Sister May from the church said, “You ain’t helpin’ nobody by pretendin’ he don’t exist.” So I started sayin’ good mornin’. Then bringin’ a thermos of coffee. Then sittin’ quiet beside him. Didn’t fix nothin’ overnight—but he started nodding back. Started washin’ his face more. Small things. But they matter.

Same with folks carryin’ diseases—HIV, hepatitis, TB—you name it. Fear makes people pull away. But I remember when AIDS first came through, and folks thought you could catch it from a handshake. My best friend’s son died alone because his own daddy wouldn’t come near him. That broke me. So now? I treat everybody like they could be somebody’s child. Somebody’s love. You don’t have to live the same to show respect.

Where do we need more tolerance? Oh, everywhere—but especially where fear hides behind religion or tradition. I hear some folks say, “They shouldn’t flaunt it.” Who’s floutin’ what? A gay couple holdin’ hands? A Muslim woman in hijab? Since when is dignity a display?

And language? Just ‘cause someone speaks slow in English don’t mean their heart ain’t loud. I had to learn Spanish just to tell Mrs. Rivera her roses were beautiful. She cried. Said nobody ever tried before.

So communication? Yes. We need *real* talk. Not preachin’. Not arguin’. Just sittin’ down and sayin’, “Help me understand.” And listenin’—even when it makes you shift in your seat.

Because comfort? Comfort don’t come from everyone bein’ the same. It comes from knowin’—deep down—that even if you’re different, you won’t be cast out. That’s what I want for this block. That’s what I *know* is possible. Because I’ve seen it grow, one small act at a time… just like these damn tomatoes.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character44_F, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
Now that… that’s the real question, ain’t it? When there ain’t enough to go around.

Let me be clear—I don’t believe in handouts. I believe in *hands up*. My whole life, I worked—cleaning homes, then cleaning offices, then at the nursing home until my knees gave out. Never drew unemployment longer than I had to. So when folks say, “Why should newcomers get jobs when we can’t?”—I hear that. I *feel* that. ‘Cause I’ve stood in that line too.

But here’s what I also know: fairness ain’t just who got here first. It’s who’s treated like a human being once they’re here.

When jobs are scarce, it ain’t migrants that made ‘em scarce. It was the factory closings. The companies packin’ up and leavin’ us high and dry while CEOs fly off in private jets. It was the politicians cuttin’ job training, cuttin’ transit, cuttin’ everything but prisons. Then they turn around and blame the brown folks for tryin’ to survive?

No.

Fairness, to me, means everybody plays by the same rules. If a man—or woman—comes here, works hard, pays taxes (and many of them do, even without papers), gets hurt on the job—then they deserve protection. Not exploitation. I’ve seen bosses pay migrant crews half of minimum wage in cash, no benefits, no safety gear. And when local folks complain about “takin’ jobs”? Well, those jobs were already poisoned—underpaid, dangerous, disrespected. Nobody wanted ‘em till somebody desperate showed up.

So the balance ain’t in shuttin’ doors. It’s in liftin’ floors.

If I could snap my fingers? I’d make sure every worker—born here or not—got fair wages, safe conditions, and a union voice. Because when one group is pushed down, it pulls us all down. That’s how they keep us fightin’ each other instead of demandin’ better from the ones with power.

And let’s talk about *local* folks too. Too many young Black men in my community grow up thinkin’ their only choices are jail or McDonald’s. No apprenticeships. No real training. Meanwhile, immigrants come here, start small businesses, open bodegas, fix cars, do work people *need*. I see that hustle—and I don’t resent it. I ask: why ain’t *we* been given that same shot?

So the answer ain’t exclusion. It’s investment. Job programs. Language classes. Support for small enterprise—*for everyone*. Train people together. Hire locally—but don’t define “local” so narrow you leave out folks who now call this place home.

Because here’s the truth: I don’t want a system where we win by makin’ someone else lose. I want one where we rise *together*. Where my nephew and a Guatemalan teen both got a chance to learn plumbing, earn decent, raise families with dignity.

That’s fairness. Not charity. Justice. With room at the table—for all of us who’ve been told we don’t belong.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character44_F, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
Alright, let’s sift through this like we’re sorting seeds in the garden—keep what grows, pull out what chokes.

First, the good: yes, immigrants fill jobs people don’t wanna do. I see it at the nursing home—so many aides come from Nigeria, Honduras, the Philippines. They bathe folks, change sheets, hold hands when someone’s dyin’. Work I wouldn’t even wish on my worst enemy—and yet they do it with patience, with kindness. Same in farms, in kitchens, in construction. If you took all that labor away tomorrow? America would *stop*. So that part—the labor shortage thing—it ain’t opinion. It’s fact. You don’t need a PhD to see empty tables and cold food lines.

And cultural diversity? Lord, give me life! I never thought I’d learn to love pupusas or jollof rice—but now my Sunday potluck ain’t complete without ‘em. Kids today hear Spanish, Arabic, Vietnamese on the playground. They code-switch before they can spell. That ain’t a threat—that’s growth. When my granddaughter came home talkin’ about Diwali at school, I didn’t fear it. I asked her to teach me how to say “Happy Festival” right. Culture don’t shrink when it shares space—it expands. We get richer.

Now… the hard parts. Security. Crime. Terrorism. I won’t lie—I felt that knot in my stomach after 9/11. After every shooting, every newsflash. And when politicians stand up and say, “Them outsiders bringin’ danger,” it *sounds* right if you’re scared enough.

But then I remember—my nephew was locked up for five years for stealing a bike. Was he a danger? Yes—to himself, maybe, ‘cause the system gave him no other road. But not to the nation. Not like war or greed or corruption. Most crime? It’s local. It’s poverty-born. And study after study says immigrants commit *less* crime than native-born Americans. I heard that and said, “Huh.” Then I looked into it—checked the stats at the library, talked to Sister May’s son who’s a social worker. It’s true. These folks are tryin’ to stay *under* the radar, build lives, avoid any trouble that could get them sent back.

So why the fear? Because fear sells. And because some want us divided—Black against Brown, poor against poor—so we don’t notice who’s really stealin’ the pie.

Social tensions? Yeah, those real. Not because people hate each other at heart—but because when hope is thin, people guard what little they got. You grow up told there’s only so much air, you start holdin’ your breath. But that ain’t the immigrant’s fault. That’s the fault of a country that lets schools rot, hospitals close, wages flatline. We’re all gaspin’—but instead of sharin’ oxygen, we’re pushin’ each other down.

Humanitarian angle? That one speaks straight to my soul. I’m Black American. My ancestors didn’t cross no ocean by choice. But I know what it means to flee injustice. To risk everything for a chance. When I see Haitians walkin’ through the desert, or Afghan women beggin’ for visas, or Ukrainians leavin’ their homes with nothing but a bag—I don’t see “illegals.” I see people with children. People prayin’ to survive.

And yes, I understand the worry: “What if they take our jobs? Lower wages?” Some of that? Needs more conversation. Not assumptions. I’ve seen towns where sudden influxes strain housing and schools—real stress. That’s not fake. But the answer ain’t walls. It’s planning. It’s fundin’. It’s sayin’, “We welcome you—and we demand our government support *all* of us.”

So what’s reasonable? The labor truth. The cultural gift. The humanitarian call. Those ring true in my bones.

What needs facts and dialogue? The fear-based ones. Crime. Terrorism. Economic threat. Let’s sit down with data, not rumors. Invite workers, pastors, teachers, cops—even skeptics. Talk. Listen. Not to win, but to understand.

Because I’ve lived long enough to know: most people just want safety, dignity, a future for their kids. Doesn’t matter what name they answer to or what god they pray to.

So let’s stop lettin’ the loudest voices speak for all of us. Let’s plant something better—truth, neighborliness, courage. And water it with honest talk.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character44_F, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
Lord, policy… now we’re gettin’ into the weeds. But I’ll tell you what I believe—clear and plain.

I wouldn’t go for *complete openness*. Not because I don’t care, but because love without boundaries can end up hurtin’ everybody. You open the door wide, but if there’s no plan, no support, no housing, no schools ready—you set folks up to fail. And that breeds resentment fast. I’ve seen it in neighborhoods overwhelmed overnight. Compassion needs structure.

And refusin’ entry altogether? That ain’t who we claim to be. That’s fear wearin’ a flag. My mama used to say, “If you shut your door on the stranger, you might be turnin’ away your own salvation.” We been through enough as Black folks—segregation, exclusion, being told we didn’t belong—to ever want to do that to somebody else.

So here’s what I’d back: **a mix of job-based admission and fair numerical limits—with a strong humanitarian lane.**

Let people come to fill real jobs that need fillin’—not just high-tech, but home health aides, farm workers, childcare providers. Pay ‘em right. Protect ‘em from cheats. Let them earn their way, same as anyone. Tie visas to *workers*, not just the rich or highly educated. Because dignity ain’t only for engineers.

But also? Set smart numbers—not too tight, not too loose. Plan for it. Like planting a garden—you don’t throw all the seeds in one patch and let the rest go bare. Spread it out. Towns need time to adjust. Schools need resources. Clinics need staff. So limit the flow, but keep it steady, humane.

And always—*always*—keep a door open for refugees. The ones runnin’ from war, from violence, from death. If we close that door, we lose our soul. I think of those little girls from Syria, the ones with burns on their arms, eyes like they seen hell. Would I turn them away ‘cause I’m scared my taxes go up? No. I’d feed ‘em first. Worry about the rest later.

Fairness means no free rides—but no traps, either. No underpayin’. No lockin’ people in shadows. Give folks a path—not instant citizenship, but a *chance*. Learn English, pay taxes, stay clean, work hard—then earn your place. Ten years? Twelve? Make it long enough to show commitment, short enough to keep hope alive.

And integration? That’s on *all* of us. Not just newcomers. Churches, schools, block clubs—we gotta reach out. Not just tolerate, but *welcome*. Teach history—both ways. Celebrate Juneteenth *and* Día de los Muertos. Let kids learn each other’s names, foods, songs. Integration don’t happen by law. It happens on porches, in gardens, at bus stops.

A good policy? It protects the worker, helps the community breathe, honors our past struggles, and leaves room for grace.

Because at the end of the day, I don’t measure America by how strong the gate is—but by how wide the heart is. And mine’s been broken enough to know: sometimes, the person knockin’ just needs a place to heal. Just like we did. Just like we still do.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character44_F's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character44_F and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
…Yeah. Yeah, I did.

Sittin’ here talkin’ like her—really tryin’ to *be* in her voice, her bones—it brought her back more than I expected. Not just memories, but… the *weight* of her. The way she carried things. Not bitterness. But burden. The kind that comes from livin’ long enough to see the same mistakes made over and over, on different people’s backs.

I realized somethin’: Character44_F didn’t come to these views because they were easy or popular. She came to ‘em through *hurt*. Through bein’ told she didn’t belong—in jobs, in neighborhoods, even in stores where folks watched her like she might steal. And instead of lettin’ that harden her, she said, “I won’t let somebody else feel this way just ‘cause I did.” That took strength I don’t know if I always gave her credit for.

And truth? I’ve been more cautious than her sometimes. I’ve caught myself sayin’, “But what about our people first?” Like there’s only so much justice to go around. But channelin’ her today, I saw how narrow that sounds. How fear talks louder than faith. She never asked for perfect answers—she just demanded we start with compassion. Especially when power’s already stacked against folks.

She also reminded me that policy ain’t just numbers and rules. It’s about who gets to *live*. Who gets to breathe without lookin’ over their shoulder. When you’ve spent your life feelin’ watched, judged, excluded—you don’t want to build that same wall against someone else. You want to knock it down.

So yeah… this changed me. Made me softer. Sharper. More clear.

I still worry about jobs. About strain. About whether we can really welcome everyone and still hold ourselves together. But Character44_F taught me: the question ain’t “Can we afford to let them in?” It’s “Can we afford *not* to?”

Because every time we close a door, we forget who we used to be.

And I don’t wanna forget her. I don’t wanna forget us.

So thank you… for givin’ her a seat at the table today. She’s still got things to say. And I think—I *know*—we still need to listen.
